question: Under what exact condition does the Java compiler automatically generate a default constructor for a class?

options.text: Whenever the class contains uninitialized blank final fields that require zeroing.
Only when the class declares at least one explicit no-argument constructor.
For every Java class regardless of what constructors the programmer declares.
Only when the programmer declares zero constructors in the class definition.

explanation: The Java compiler automatically generates a default constructor if and only if no constructor is explicitly declared in the class. If any constructor is declared, no default constructor is provided.

question: What access modifier does the compiler-generated default constructor receive in Java?

options.text: It is always package-private even when the class is declared public.
It is always public regardless of the access modifier on the declaring class.
It is always protected so that subclasses can inherit it.
It receives the exact same access modifier as the declaring class itself.

explanation: The default constructor has the same access level as its declaring class: if the class is public, the default constructor is public; if the class has package-private access, the constructor has package-private access.

question: What does the body of a compiler-generated default constructor contain?

options.text: It initializes all primitive fields to zero and all object references to empty instances.
It contains a call to this(0) to chain with user-defined constructors.
It contains an implicit invocation of super() delegating to the superclass no-argument constructor.
It is completely empty with no bytecode instructions whatsoever.

explanation: The compiler-generated default constructor has an empty body containing only a single call to super(), invoking the no-argument constructor of the superclass.

question: Which statement accurately distinguishes a programmer-written no-argument constructor from the default constructor in Java?

options.text: Any programmer-written zero-argument constructor is technically defined as the default constructor.
The default constructor refers strictly to the compiler-generated constructor created in the absence of explicit constructors.
Programmer-written zero-argument constructors always receive public visibility automatically.
The compiler-generated constructor always overrides programmer-written zero-argument constructors.

explanation: In Java terminology, the default constructor is specifically the zero-argument constructor generated automatically by the compiler when no constructors are written. An explicitly written constructor with zero parameters is a user-defined no-argument constructor.

question: Suppose class InternalPackageClass is defined with package-private access in package com.data, and class Main in package com.app attempts to access and instantiate it using new InternalPackageClass(). Which statement correctly describes the compile-time failure?

options.text: InternalPackageClass is not public in com.data and cannot be accessed from outside its package (the default constructor of a package-private class is also package-private).
InternalPackageClass default constructor is uninitialized because no fields exist
InternalPackageClass cannot have a default constructor across package boundaries
InternalPackageClass default constructor is always public and can be accessed anywhere

explanation: The default constructor inherits the accessibility of its declaring class. Because InternalPackageClass has package-private access in package com.data, both the class and its default constructor cannot be accessed from package com.app, resulting in a compilation error.
